author: ohtadmin
title: State: Coastal storms still dangerous
text:
Alerts by police to expect road closures and warnings from environmentalists about potential “life-threatening rip tides” preceded what eventually would become a lackluster passage of Rhode Island by Hurricane Erin.
The storm was at its height last Thursday into Friday as spectators crowded Beavertail Point to see the forecasted 10-foot waves crash against the cliffs. They were instead greeted by less significant splashes as Erin passed well out to sea.
Emergency management officials, however, used the event as a reminder for coastal homeowners to remain vigilant as future storms might not be as tame.
Federal forecasters at both the National Weather Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration are predicting a “busier than average” hurricane season. Using those forecasts as a barometer, the Rhode Island Coastal Resources Management Council said its website offers resources for property owners, both in preparation of hurricanes and in post-storm assessments.
Although Rhode Island has not experienced “a severe hurricane” since the 1950s, and Hurricane Bob in 1991 was the last to make landfall in the Ocean State, CRMC executive director Jeff Willis is advising residents to listen to forecasts rather than rely on seasonal predictions.
“Meteorologists do a great job of explaining where and when active storms are happening and how they may impact our coastline,” he said.
“Hurricanes and tropical storms are likely to increase in intensity,” added Emily Hall, a coastal geologist with the agency.
“As sea level rises, both hurricanes and nor’easters will be more damaging, and the flooding effects will be felt farther inland. Storm surge and wave heights will increase as sea level rises,” she said, “resulting in more properties being damaged or destroyed during a storm.”
Willis said his agency can issue emergency permits to address storm-related damage. They are declared at the discretion of the executive director and generally are declared when there are “widespread and significant impacts to human health and safety.” The last time an emergency permit was declared was following Superstorm Sandy in 2012. Emergency declarations at the municipal, state and federal levels are independent of the coastal agency.
Although not present during Erin, in the case of significant damage, property owners are encouraged to contact their local building official to have an evaluation done after a storm. If a septic system is exposed or damaged, Willis recommends contacting the state’s Department of Environmental Management for an assessment. Permits are needed for any repairs or movement of the structure.
For any necessary minor repairs, homeowners could qualify for a maintenance permit from the CRMC. For structures that have incurred more than 50 percent damage, which can be determined by a local building official in cooperation with the agency, property owners must submit a full assent application to Willis’ agency.
Hurricane season typically is from June through November. Hurricanes in the northern hemisphere have a counterclockwise rotation, so a hurricane tracking to the east of Rhode Island is considered preferable. If a storm were to track to the west, the rotation of the storm would reinforce the forward motion of the storm. However, since Erin was tracking to the east, winds were moving in the offshore direction, and there was comparably less flooding.
Jamestown’s police department has published a two-page brochure to prepare residents for severe storms. The brochure, titled “Hurricane Preparedness Tips,” includes directions on creating an emergency kit and developing a family emergency plan. The brochure can be found at Town Hall, the department’s Facebook page and the municipal website.
